props.title: Cosmopolis
props.initialSlug: A billionaire's surreal limo ride into chaos

sections.content: **Cosmopolis** (2012) represents David Cronenberg's most clinical dissection of late-stage capitalism, adapting Don DeLillo's novel into a claustrophobic limousine odyssey across Manhattan. Like **American Psycho** (2000) before it, the film uses a wealthy protagonist to expose the hollow core of financial excess. Robert Pattinson delivers a deliberately alienating performance as Eric Packer, a 28-year-old billionaire whose empire crumbles during a single day's journey. The film's confined setting recalls **Locke** (2013), another one-location character study, but Cronenberg's version is far more experimental and abstract.

movies.title: The Wolf of Wall Street
movies.slug: Scorsese's manic portrayal of financial excess and collapse through Jordan Belfort's true story

sections.content: Cronenberg's signature body horror takes on a different form here - instead of physical transformation, we witness the decay of humanity through digital abstraction. The sterile environment of Packer's high-tech limousine echoes similar confined spaces in **Ex Machina** (2014) and **High-Rise** (2015), where technology and wealth create isolated bubbles that eventually implode. The film's prophetic vision of financial collapse and civil unrest feels especially relevant post-2008 crash, joining films like **Margin Call** (2011) and **Inside Job** (2010) in examining systemic economic rot.

The film's deliberately paced descent into chaos mirrors Packer's psychological unraveling. Like **Fight Club** (1999), it shows a man trapped in the system he helped create, though Packer never achieves Tyler Durden's anarchic liberation. The clinical dialogue and artificial performances connect to Cronenberg's earlier work like **Crash** (1996), where human connection is mediated through technology and violence. movies.title: Killing Them Softly
movies.slug: Brad Pitt stars in this cynical crime drama about capitalism and the 2008 financial collapse

sections.content: Cronenberg joins other filmmakers using horror techniques to explore economic anxiety. **Possessor** (2020), directed by his son Brandon Cronenberg, continues this tradition of body horror as corporate infiltration. **The Big Short** (2015) turns financial instruments into instruments of horror, while **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) pushes capitalist exploitation into surreal body horror territory. These films recognize that traditional monster movies can't match the terror of market forces.
